Literas tamen hodiernas (optas à Græcis deri-

Cùm enim multa Græcorum colonie in
Ægyptum migrâssent, præsertim post Alexandr.
Magnum, & temporibus Ptolemæorum Græ-
corum qui per 300 annos in Ægypto regnâ-
runt, dubitari non potest linguam Græcam per
Ægyptum multum propagatam fuisse. Imò
ante Alexandrum, Psammetichum Ægypti
Regem memorat Herodotus in Euterpe,
Græcorum millia, Ionesc. & Cares in
Ægyptum admisisse, & pueros Ægyptiacos ipsis in-
stituendos tradidisse. Ἀπὸ [?]ῆ τῶν ἐκμαθόντων τὴν Ἑλλάδα γλῶσσαν,
οἱ νῦν ἑρμηνεῖς ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ γεγόνασι. Et ab his linguam Græcam edoctis,
ortos qui nunc in Ægpto interpretes, ut idem
Herodotus. Post Ptolemæos etiam altas radices
egit in Ægypto Græca lingua, adeo ut Coptorum
dialectus hodie multò plura habeat Græca vo-
cabula quam Ægyptiaca.
87 Causa statuunt duplicem mutationis anti-
quæ linguæ Coptæ seu Ægyptiacæ; prima fuit
Cambysis tyrannis, qui Ægyptum subjugavit
& omnia literarum monumenta delere conatus est,

page.notes: The main text is set in italic type throughout, with some roman words; I have marked the body paragraphs as italic and did not separate individual roman words. Doubtful readings: "ἧ" in the Greek sentence and "Ionesc." (the printed abbreviation after "Iones" is hard to read; "Ionesfc." is printed as the abbreviation of &c.). The Greek "αὐτογενέσι" and the Latin "apleris[?]que" are uncertain readings; the word "apleris" appears as printed on the scan. The catchword "est," is the last word of the page and runs into the following page.
